cards.text: Friend, Nahum is a prophet, and his whole message is aimed at one city: Nineveh (Nahum 1:1). Last chapter, an army was charging through its streets (Nahum 2:1-4). Now Nahum cries out, 'Woe,' and he calls Nineveh the city of blood.

cards.question: Nahum calls Nineveh the city of blood. What else does he say the city is full of?

cards.text: Then Nahum makes you HEAR it. The crack of the whip, the rumble of the wheel, horses galloping, chariots bounding, horsemen charging, swords flashing, spears shining!

cards.question: After the charging horsemen and the flashing swords, what does Nahum describe next?
Nahum says the dead bodies are without end, so many that they stumble over their dead.

cards.text: Then Nahum gives the reason for all of it. He pictures Nineveh as a harlot, a seductive mistress of sorcery.

cards.question: Nahum says this mistress of sorcery ___ nations and clans.

cards.text: Now the LORD of Hosts Himself speaks. And He opens with the same words He used at the end of the last chapter (Nahum 2:13).

cards.question: The LORD of Hosts tells Nineveh, "Behold, I am ___ you."
The LORD says He will show Nineveh's shame. Who does He say will see it?

answers.text: Her king and no one else

cards.text: And He keeps going. He'll pelt her with filth, treat her with contempt and make a spectacle of her.

cards.question: The LORD says everyone who sees Nineveh will recoil and say, "Nineveh is devastated; who will ___ for her?"
The LORD says Nineveh will have plenty of people to comfort her.

cards.text: Then Nahum asks Nineveh a question: are you better than Thebes? Thebes sat by the Nile with water all around her, and the water was her wall.

cards.question: Thebes had a wall of water. Who does Nahum say were her boundless strength?

cards.text: Put and Libya were her allies too. A wall of WATER and four nations in her corner? Friend, my walls in that junk drawer were takeout menus.

cards.question: With all that water and all those allies, Thebes was never captured.

cards.text: She went into exile, into captivity. Her infants were dashed to pieces at the head of every street, and all her nobles were bound in chains.

cards.question: How did the enemy decide who got Thebes's dignitaries?
Why does Nahum bring up Thebes when he's talking to Nineveh?

answers.text: Strong walls and allies didn't save her
Thebes promised to send Nineveh help

cards.text: Then Nahum turns back to Nineveh with two words: you too. She'll become drunk and go into hiding.

cards.question: Nahum says Nineveh will go into hiding and seek ___ from the enemy.

cards.text: Next, Nahum looks at all her fortresses. He calls them fig trees, loaded with the first ripe figs.

cards.question: What does Nahum say happens when those fig tree fortresses are shaken?

answers.text: The figs fall into the eater's mouth
The figs hold tight to the branches
The trees put down deeper roots

cards.text: One shake, friend. ONE. And down they go. Then Nahum turns to the gates of her land.

cards.question: Nahum says the gates of Nineveh's land are wide open to her enemies.

cards.text: Fire consumes the bars of those gates. Then Nahum tells her to get busy: draw water for the siege, strengthen the fortresses, tread the mortar and repair the brick kiln!

cards.question: Nahum tells Nineveh to strengthen her fortresses. What does he say will happen to her there?

cards.text: The sword will cut her down and consume her like a young locust. Then Nahum says, make yourself many like the young locust, many like the swarming locust!

cards.question: Nahum tells Nineveh, "You have multiplied your ___ more than the stars of the sky."

cards.text: More merchants than STARS, and my night sky is still working on its first constellation! Then Nahum says her guards are like swarming locusts, and her scribes like clouds of locusts settling on the walls on a cold day.

cards.question: Nahum pictures Nineveh's guards and scribes as locusts on the walls. What do those locusts do when the sun rises?
Nahum says everyone knows where those locusts go when they fly away.

cards.text: Guards and scribes, GONE, and no one knows where. That's everybody in the group chat when somebody asks who can help them move.
Then Nahum speaks right to the king of Assyria: his shepherds slumber and his officers sleep. The whole leadership hit SNOOZE.

cards.question: With the shepherds asleep, the king's people are ___ on the mountains.

cards.text: And there's no one to gather them. Then comes Nahum's last word to the king: there's no healing for his injury, and his wound is severe.

cards.question: When everyone hears the news about the king of Assyria, what do they do?
Nahum says all who hear the news applaud the king's downfall. Why?

answers.text: They've all felt his constant cruelty
They were all paid to cheer for it
They never knew who he was

findings.problem: "His whole message is aimed at one city: Nineveh (Nahum 1:1)" stretches the text. Nahum 1:1 calls the book "the burden against Nineveh," but Nahum also speaks to Judah (Nahum 1:12-15). Saying the whole message is aimed at one city claims more than the text says.

rule.text: Don't stretch the text. Exaggerate only in his own jokes.

findings.problem: Verse 13 opens with "Look at your troops—they are like your women!" The walkthrough leaves this out completely. Card 5 cites Nahum 3:12-13 but goes straight from the fig trees to the gates. The goal asks that the baker not miss an important detail. The hard rules forbid putting down any group, including by gender. Retelling this line could read as a gender put-down even though it is Scripture.
findings.question: Should Prep retell a verse whose comparison could read as a put-down of a group, like the troops being likened to women in Nahum 3:13? If yes, how should Papa Dorin word it so it stays faithful to the text without sounding like a gender joke? If no, may it be left out even though the goal says no important detail is missed?

findings.problem: The blank asks the baker to guess a word of Nahum 3:16 they haven't seen: merchants, temples or horses. Nothing in the earlier cards points to merchants, so the baker can only guess by luck. The card should test meaning the baker can reason out, or a story card should give enough context first.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The joke "my night sky is still working on its first constellation" states how far along the night sky is. Each sealed box lights a star, so the sky's progress may depend on how many boxes this baker has sealed, and Papa Dorin isn't told that. The line could be false for a baker who has already finished constellations. It also adds a new fact to his world.
findings.question: Is the Dorinverse night sky shared, or does it reflect each baker's own sealed boxes? Can Papa Dorin joke about how many stars or constellations it has?

findings.problem: The question says "Nahum pictures Nineveh's guards and scribes as locusts on the walls." In Nahum 3:17, only the scribes are likened to clouds of locusts that settle on the walls. The guards are likened to the swarming locust, with nothing about walls.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: This story card only repeats what card 13 just answered ("no one knows where") and adds a joke. It doesn't move the passage forward. The group chat joke should ride along on a card that tells the next piece of the passage, like card 15.

rule.text: Every story card moves the baker forward through the passage.
